newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss coffee trader sees tight 96/97 world balance.
newsitem.headline: Swiss coffee trader sees tight 96/97 world balance.

text.p: The world's exportable coffee crop is forecast to reach 4.42 million tonnes in 1996/97 (October-September), just sufficient to cover consumption of 4.41 million tonnes, a Swiss coffee trader said on Wednesday.

Hans de Heer, president of Swiss-based coffee firm Inter-Link SA, said at a seminar for small east European roasters that world production would rise to 5.85 million tonnes from a weather-affected crop of 5.11 million in 1995/96.
Last season, coffee saw a supply gap of 628,000 tonnes after a poor Brazilian harvest.
"Overall statistical situation is neutral," he said. "Without any major disruption...prices should remain at around 100-110 U.S. cents a lb."
March coffee futures on the New York market were trading at 105 cents in early Wednesday business.
De Heer said top grower Brazil alone would produce 594,000 tonnes more this season due to a recovery from the frosts and drought of 1994.
He said total disappearance (consumption) in producing countries would reach 1.43 million tonnes this season, leaving 4.42 million available for exports.

Worldwide stocks would total about 2.0 million tonnes, equivalent to six weeks of roastings. Stocks at the origins were estimated at 1.5 million tonnes and the remaining 505,000 tonnes were in roasters' hands.
Global consumption would be a stable 4.41 million tonnes in 1996/97, barely changed from 4.38 million in 1995/96.
De Heer said that while overall supply and demand would be fairly balanced, there could be imbalances in specific coffee qualities, especially in milds.
Stocks of mild coffee in consumer hands could fall by 85,000 tonnes to 290,000 tonnes at the end of this season from 375,000 at the start of the season.
But stocks of unwashed arabica coffee would rise to 230,000 tones from 120,000 tonnes in the same period, he said.
